title: What 'abatement' means (OSHA vs. prequal deficiency)
body:
"Abatement" is used in two related ways in Origin's world:

1. OSHA citation abatement: after an OSHA inspection results in a citation, the employer must correct (abate) the hazard by the "abatement date" on the citation and prove it. Failure to abate carries additional daily penalties (Failure to Abate, up to the statutory max per day).

2. Prequal-platform deficiency correction: when a RAVS / Safety Manual Audit / T-RAVS review returns a written program "not accepted," the contractor must correct the specific deficiencies the reviewer listed and resubmit. Practitioners loosely call this "abating" the deficiency.

Both share the same shape: (a) understand exactly what was cited/flagged, (b) fix it at the root, (c) DOCUMENT the fix with objective evidence, (d) submit proof in the required format, (e) verify acceptance. A fix with no documentation is treated as no fix.

title: OSHA citation abatement — the required process
body:
Steps to abate an OSHA citation:
1. Read the citation: note each item, the standard cited (29 CFR ...), the classification (Other-than-Serious / Serious / Willful / Repeat), the proposed penalty, and the ABATEMENT DATE.
2. Decide within 15 working days of receipt: pay & abate, request an informal conference with the Area Director, or file a Notice of Contest. The 15-working-day clock is strict.
3. Correct the hazard by the abatement date. Engineering controls first, then administrative controls/PPE.
4. Certify abatement: OSHA requires a signed Abatement Certification for each item, stating the date and method of correction (29 CFR 1903.19). For Serious/Willful/Repeat, or when required, attach abatement DOCUMENTATION (photos, purchase records, training rosters, work orders, corrected written program).
5. Post the citation at or near the location of each violation for 3 working days or until abated (whichever is longer).
6. If more time is needed, file a Petition for Modification of Abatement (PMA) BEFORE the abatement date expires (typically within 1 working day after the date if abatement was prevented by factors beyond control), explaining steps taken, why more time is needed, and interim protection.
7. Keep everything — OSHA can conduct a follow-up inspection.

title: Abatement certification vs. documentation vs. plan
body:
Three distinct OSHA deliverables (29 CFR 1903.19):
- Abatement CERTIFICATION: a signed statement (by the employer or an authorized representative) that the cited item has been corrected, with the date and a brief description of the action. Required for EVERY cited item.
- Abatement DOCUMENTATION: objective evidence the correction occurred — photos, invoices/receipts for equipment, work orders, training sign-in sheets, the revised written program page. Required for Willful/Repeat items and Serious items where OSHA indicates, and any time OSHA requests it.
- Abatement PLAN + progress reports: required for long-term/complex corrections that cannot be completed quickly — a written plan with milestones and interim protective measures, plus periodic progress reports.
Send certifications/documentation to the OSHA Area Office by the abatement date; keep copies.
sample_language:
ABATEMENT CERTIFICATION
Citation [#], Item [#] — 29 CFR [standard]
[Company] certifies that the violation described was corrected on [date] by the following action: [describe the specific corrective action — e.g., "installed machine guarding meeting 1910.212 on the [machine]; retrained all operators on [date]; revised the written machine-guarding program to add monthly guard inspections assigned to the Maintenance Supervisor."]. Supporting documentation is attached: [list].
Signed: __________________  Name/Title: __________  Date: ______

title: Choosing a corrective method (hierarchy of controls)
body:
OSHA and reviewers expect corrections that follow the hierarchy of controls, strongest first:
1. Elimination / substitution — remove the hazard or swap for a safer process.
2. Engineering controls — guarding, ventilation, interlocks, fall-protection anchors, GFCI.
3. Administrative controls — procedures, permits, inspection schedules, rotation.
4. PPE — last line, only when higher controls are infeasible or supplementary.
A durable abatement usually pairs an engineering/administrative fix with a WRITTEN PROGRAM UPDATE and TRAINING so the same hazard cannot recur. Reviewers reward root-cause fixes ("we added a monthly documented guard inspection assigned to X") over one-off patches ("we put the guard back on").

title: Correcting a RAVS / Safety Manual Audit / T-RAVS deficiency
body:
When a written-program review returns "not accepted," the reviewer lists SPECIFIC deficiencies. To abate:
1. Read each deficiency literally — reviewers mark an element missing if it is not literally on the page, even if implied.
2. Map each deficiency to the exact section of your program and edit that section to state the missing element explicitly (procedure, named responsible party by title, frequency, training, recordkeeping, citation).
3. Use assertive language ("{Company} will/shall...") — not "should/when feasible."
4. Make it company-specific to your actual scope of work; remove hazards/tasks you don't perform.
5. Date and version the revised program.
6. Resubmit through the platform, and where the portal allows, add a short reviewer note listing what changed and where ("Added Section 4.3 rescue plan per deficiency 2; added competent-person designation in Section 2").
7. Track it to acceptance — resubmission starts a new ~1-2 week review cycle.

title: The most common prequal deficiencies and exactly how to fix each
body:
- "Generic/template manual": rewrite in the company's voice, insert real job titles, actual equipment, and the specific procedures your crews use.
- "Responsibility unclear": replace "management is responsible" with a named role, its authority, stop-work authority, and escalation path.
- "Missing rescue plan" (Confined Space): add a section naming the rescue service/method, how it's summoned, and response-time expectation.
- "Missing periodic inspection" (LOTO): add an annual documented periodic inspection assigned to a named authorized employee.
- "No competent-person designation" (Fall Protection/Excavation/Scaffold): name the competent person and their duties/authority.
- "Training frequency/documentation missing": state who is trained, by whom, initial + refresher frequency, and how completion is recorded and retained.
- "Wrong/missing citation": add the correct 29 CFR citation for the topic.
- "Non-assertive language": change should/may to will/shall.
- "Scope mismatch / over-committed": delete tasks and hazards the company doesn't actually have.
- Insurance deficiency: obtain a corrected COI with the required limits/endorsements or a carrier-issued EMR letter; re-upload.

title: Building an abatement evidence package that survives review
body:
A strong abatement package pairs the FIX with PROOF:
- Before/after photos with dates.
- Invoices/receipts/work orders for equipment or engineering controls.
- The revised written-program page(s) showing the added element.
- Training rosters with individual names, dates, trainer, and topic.
- Inspection/audit records showing the new control operating (a closed corrective-action log entry is powerful).
- A one-page corrective-action summary: hazard/deficiency -> root cause -> action taken -> date -> responsible person -> evidence attached.
For prequal platforms, the reviewer wants proof of IMPLEMENTATION, not just a revised policy — the closed corrective action and training roster are what turn "policy exists" into "program is operating" in the reviewer's eyes.

title: Writing a corrective-action response to a citation or over-threshold metric
body:
When a citation or an over-threshold TRIR/EMR is flagged, a documented corrective-action plan often keeps a contractor hireable even while the number is high. Structure:
1. What happened (the citation/recordable), stated plainly and without minimizing.
2. Root cause (why it happened — the system gap, not "employee error").
3. Corrective actions taken (specific, by the hierarchy of controls), with dates.
4. Preventive actions (program update, training, new inspection) so it can't recur.
5. Responsible person and completion/verification date.
An over-threshold EMR/TRIR with a credible corrective-action narrative reads far better than a good number with no explanation — and a bad number with NO explanation is what actually gets a contractor filtered out.
sample_language:
CORRECTIVE ACTION SUMMARY
Event: [citation / recordable injury on date]
Root cause: [system gap — e.g., "no documented pre-task hazard assessment for elevated work"]
Corrective actions: [1) installed anchor points meeting 1926.502 on [date]; 2) implemented mandatory pre-task JSA; 3) retrained all field crews [date]].
Preventive/systemic: [revised Fall Protection Program to require weekly documented harness inspections assigned to the Site Supervisor].
Responsible: [name/title]. Verified complete: [date].

title: Tracking abatements to closure (Draft -> Approved -> Uploaded -> Verified)
body:
Every abatement should move through a status ladder so nothing stalls before a deadline:
- Draft: correction + documentation being assembled.
- Approved: internally reviewed and signed off (management certification ready).
- Uploaded/Submitted: sent to OSHA Area Office or resubmitted in the prequal portal.
- Verified: acceptance confirmed (OSHA acknowledgment, or platform status returned to compliant/green/approved).
Track for each item: the deadline (OSHA abatement date or portal resubmit target), the responsible owner, and the evidence attached. The #1 avoidable failure is missing the abatement date or letting a resubmission sit — set the deadline as the driving field. Origin's abatement module implements exactly this ladder file-based; use it rather than a spreadsheet.

title: Deadlines and pitfalls that turn an abatement into a bigger problem
body:
- OSHA 15-working-day window to contest/confer runs from receipt — miss it and the citation becomes a final order.
- Abatement date is firm; if you can't meet it, file a PMA BEFORE it lapses with interim protection described.
- "Failure to Abate" penalties accrue PER DAY — an ignored abatement can dwarf the original penalty.
- Certification is required for every item even for quick fixes; skipping it looks like non-abatement.
- For prequal: resubmitting the SAME program without addressing the literal deficiencies just burns another review cycle.
- Fixing the instance but not the system (no program update/training) invites a Repeat citation, which carries much higher penalties and a lasting grade hit.
- Never backdate documentation — mismatched dates between photos, invoices, and certifications are an audit red flag.
